assistant:
The plot shows a weak positive tendency — prices are generally a bit higher in the 1500–1700 m range than at lower altitudes around 1200–1300 m, where a notable cluster of points sits between roughly $5–7/kg. However, the relationship is quite noisy, with wide price variation at every altitude, and some of the highest prices (~$10/kg) appear at both low and mid altitudes.

Based on this plot alone, higher altitude land offers a modest advantage in expected price, but it is far from a reliable predictor. The cooperative would be reasonable to favour higher-altitude plots, but should not treat altitude as the deciding factor given the substantial scatter throughout.

Breaking out by varietal reveals that the earlier altitude story was largely a varietal story in disguise. Typica (yellow) dominates the higher altitudes and commands consistently higher prices (~$7–10/kg), while Bourbon (purple) is concentrated at lower altitudes with noticeably lower prices (~$5–7/kg). Caturra (teal) sits in between on both dimensions.

This means the cooperative should think carefully about **which varietal to plant** as much as which altitude to buy at — Typica appears to be the stronger driver of higher prices. If they plant Bourbon at high altitude, this plot gives no strong reason to expect the same premium that Typica fetches there.
